title: Philemon
subtitle: a letter about one slave, read aloud to a whole church
lead: Philemon is the shortest of Paul's letters, 25 verses and about 335 words in Greek. Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a believer whose house was the meeting place of a church, probably at Colossae in Phrygia. He writes about Onesimus, a slave of Philemon's household, who has come to faith through Paul while Paul was in chains and is now going home carrying this letter.

Paul does not command. He appeals, as an old man and a prisoner, for his "child." He asks Philemon to have Onesimus back "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother," to welcome him "as if he were me," and to charge any debt to Paul's account. He signs the promise to pay in his own hand, and says he knows Philemon will do even more than he asks.

The letter is warm, witty and carefully argued, with puns on the slave's name, which means "Useful." It is also the place where the Bible's slavery question is sharpest. Paul sends a slave back to his master and does not say "set him free." He also tells the master that his slave is now his brother. For centuries readers have argued over what Paul asked for, and the letter was used both to defend American slavery and to attack it.
facts: Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender (1:1). Paul writes in the first person throughout and signs a promise in his own hand (1:19).
The mid-50s if written from prison in Ephesus (Lightfoot dates Paul's stay there to about AD 54-57); about AD 57-62 if from Caesarea or Rome. See the deep dive on the chapter page.
Paul in prison, with Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke around him. Philemon and the church in his house, most likely at Colossae in the Lycus valley of Phrygia (Colossians 4:9, 17).
A personal letter of request, addressed also to a house church and meant to be read aloud. It has the shape of an ancient letter: greeting, thanksgiving, request, greetings and blessing.
1 chapter, 25 verses (334 words in the SBL Greek text)
Colossians, which names the same people (Onesimus, Archippus, Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Luke, Demas) and was carried by Tychicus with Onesimus (Colossians 4:7-17).
authorship: Paul wrote it from prison, as it says. The church of the 100s accepted it: Marcion kept it in his edited collection, Tertullian commented on it, and the Muratorian Fragment lists "one to Philemon." In the 300s some denied that Paul wrote it, or said it held nothing to build readers up; Jerome, Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia answered them, as Lightfoot shows from their own words.

Philemon is one of the seven letters that nearly all scholars accept as Paul's own (with Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians and 1 Thessalonians). In the 1800s F. C. Baur of Tübingen, who accepted only four letters, doubted it and called it perhaps a "Christian romance" meant to teach an idea; his view is now regarded as outdated. The style, the names shared with Colossians, and the plain personal occasion all fit Paul.

audience.to: Philemon, a believer who owned a house large enough for a church to meet in and owned at least one slave, with Apphia (probably his wife), Archippus (perhaps their son, or a church leader) and the church that met in the house (1:1-2). Colossians places Onesimus and Archippus at Colossae, a small town in the Lycus valley of Phrygia, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 4:9, 13, 17). The church there was founded by Epaphras, not by Paul (Colossians 1:7), but Philemon owed his faith to Paul (1:19), perhaps from Paul's years at Ephesus. If Philemon did as Paul asked, the church in his house would hold a master and his slave as brothers (1:16).
audience.why: Onesimus, a slave of the household, had come to Paul in prison and become a believer, and Paul was sending him home. Paul writes so that Philemon will receive him not as a returning slave to be punished or simply put back to work, but as a brother, and as Paul himself. He offers to pay any loss, and hints at more. Because the letter is addressed to the church as well, the whole congregation would hear the request and see the response. Knowing the audience changes the reading: this is not a treatise on slavery but a request to one master, in front of his church, about one man whom Paul loves.
views: Onesimus had fled, perhaps after a theft, met Paul in prison, and is now being returned with a plea for mercy (Chrysostom; Lightfoot).
Onesimus fled to Paul for protection, drawing on the ancient practice of asylum (one of the five views Tolmie counts).
Onesimus went to Paul, a friend of his master, to plead his case after some offense, which Roman jurists did not count as running away (Lampe and others, from Digest 21.1.17.4).
A slave sent to help Paul
Philemon or the church had sent Onesimus to Paul, and Paul is asking to keep him, or for his freedom.
Onesimus was an erro, a slave who drifted about without truly fleeing (Tolmie's fifth view).
Onesimus was Philemon's estranged brother, and the letter seeks to reconcile them (Callahan); or nothing proves he was a slave at all (Barnes).

outline: Greeting from Paul the prisoner and Timothy to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in the house
Thanks for Philemon's love and faith, which have set the saints' hearts at rest
The appeal for Onesimus: once useless, now useful; sent back, to be had back forever as a brother
"Welcome him as if he were me": Paul's signed promise to pay, his confidence, and his coming visit
Greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke, and the blessing

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the letter in its world: Roman slavery and the law on runaways and on slaves who sought out their master's friend (Digest 21.1), Pliny's letter for a freedman, a house church at Colossae in Phrygia, the names shared with Colossians and Acts, and the question of where Paul was imprisoned.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks the scholars' questions: the near-universal acceptance of the letter as Paul's (and Baur's dissent), what the occasion was (runaway, mediator, sent helper, estranged brother), what Paul asked for, the text and its variants, John Knox's theory about Onesimus and the collection of Paul's letters, and why a private letter was kept.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the art of persuasion: the request instead of a command, the appeals to standing and to feeling, the name held to the end, the puns on Onesimus ("Useful"), the business words (partner, account, repay) and family words (child, brother, sister), the crossed order of 1:5 and the three "hearts" (1:7, 1:12, 1:20).

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Paul as a Jewish teacher: the Torah's law against returning a runaway slave (Deuteronomy 23:15-16) and its rabbinic readings (Talmud Gittin 45a; Rashi), the Hebrew slave laws (Exodus 21; Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15) and the slave who stays "for life," and the teacher who "fathers" disciples.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Follows the letter through the church: Tertullian and Marcion, Jerome, Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia defending it, the bishop Onesimus of Ignatius, Aquinas, Luther's "We are all his Onesimi," Calvin, Wesley, the American slavery debate (Charles Colcock Jones, Albert Barnes, Richard Fuller) and present teaching such as the Catholic Catechism 2414.

sections.b:
Read it aloud, the way it was first heard, in a house full of people. Notice who "you" is: the whole church in the greeting (1:3), Philemon alone from 1:4 to 1:21, and everyone again at the end (1:22, 1:25). Notice how long Paul waits before he names Onesimus (1:10) and before he makes his request in plain words (1:17). Notice the business words and the family words, which make the request feel like both a contract and a family matter.

Then read it with Colossians 4:7-18 beside it. The same people send greetings, Onesimus travels with Tychicus, and Archippus receives a word of his own. The two letters were carried together to the same town.

The notes mark the places where English hides the Greek: the puns on the name Onesimus (1:11, 1:20), the word splanchna, "heart" (1:7, 1:12, 1:20), "old man" or "ambassador" (1:9), and "no longer as a slave" (1:16).

sections.h: Slaves, masters and runaways in Roman law
sections.b:
In the Roman world a slave was property. A slave who ran away was a fugitivus; he could be hunted, and anyone who sheltered him could be liable to his owner. But the Roman jurists made a distinction that may bear on this letter. A slave who, fearing a beating, ran to a friend of his master to get him to plead was not counted as a fugitive (Ulpian, quoting earlier jurists, in Digest 21.1.17.4; and Paul the jurist, 21.1.43.1, which says in our translation, "one who flees to a friend of his master to plead is not a fugitive").

Pliny the Younger's letter to Sabinianus (Letters 9.21) shows what such a plea looked like. A freedman who had angered his patron came to Pliny in tears; Pliny wrote asking his friend to forgive him, and said he feared his letter might seem not to ask but to compel. A later letter (9.24) thanks Sabinianus for taking the man back. Lightfoot printed Pliny's letter beside Philemon. The likeness is clear, and so is the difference: Pliny asks for pardon for a penitent dependent, while Paul asks that a slave be received as a brother and as Paul himself, and offers to pay.

sections.h: The Torah and the runaway slave
sections.b:
Israel's law took the opposite line from most ancient law: "Do not hand a slave over to his master when he has escaped from his master to you" (Deuteronomy 23:15). The escaped slave is to live where he chooses, and "Do not mistreat him" (Deuteronomy 23:16). The Talmud records several readings: a slave who fled from abroad into the land of Israel, a slave sold to a master abroad, a slave bought in order to be freed, and a Gentile who had given up idols (Gittin 45a). Rashi took the first, that it covers even an Israelite's slave who fled from outside the land into it.

Paul does not cite Deuteronomy, and he sends Onesimus back. Readers have asked whether this breaks the spirit of the law. Some answer that Paul was not handing Onesimus over to harm but asking for his welcome, with his own credit as a guarantee, and that Onesimus may well have gone willingly. Others think Paul simply accepted Roman practice. The note on 1:12 and the spec box on the chapter page take this further.

We do not know what Philemon did. The letter was kept, which suggests that it was honored. Colossians 4:9 sends Onesimus home as "the faithful and beloved brother." Some decades later, Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to martyrdom in Rome, thanked the church of Ephesus for its bishop, "Onesimus, a man of inexpressible love" (To the Ephesians 1). John Knox (Philemon among the Letters of Paul, 1935) argued that this was the same man, now old, and that as bishop he helped gather Paul's letters, which would explain why this little letter survived. Lightfoot, writing earlier, thought it possible but unlikely, since Ignatius seems to speak of a younger man and the name was common among slaves. Later legends made Onesimus a bishop of Beroea (Apostolic Constitutions 7.46) or a martyr in Rome.

The two letters share a cast: Timothy as co-sender, Onesimus, Archippus, Epaphras, Aristarchus, Mark, Luke and Demas (Colossians 1:1; 4:9-17). Colossians adds Tychicus as the letter carrier and Jesus called Justus, and gives Epaphras and Aristarchus the title "fellow captive" in opposite places. Colossians 4:7-9 implies that the two letters traveled together, with Tychicus and Onesimus. The household rules of Colossians 3:22-4:1 tell slaves to obey and masters to be just; Philemon shows one master being asked for much more.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Onesimus is the letter's answer to "useful"
spec.body: This is my own reading, built on observations by Lightfoot and Robertson. Paul plays on the name Onesimus twice ("useless... useful," 1:11; "let me gain something from you," 1:20). I think the whole request turns on what "useful" means. To an owner, a slave is useful as property: labor, value, a sum that can be lost (1:18). Paul redefines it: Onesimus is now useful "to you and to me," as one who serves the good news (1:13), as a brother (1:16), and as the means by which Philemon can "profit" Paul in the Lord (1:20). The slave's name, given for his value as property, becomes a description of his worth as a person in Christ. The same word, euchrēstos, is used later of Mark (2 Timothy 4:11), who had once been left behind. The puns themselves are noted by Lightfoot and Robertson; reading the whole request through them is my own.

prompts: The letter read in a house church

A hand-drawn scroll scene in ink and earth colors: a low-ceilinged room in a modest Roman-era house, men, women and children seated on mats and benches, an older man in a good cloak holding a small papyrus letter as another man reads it aloud, and a young man in a plain tunic standing in the doorway with a traveler's bag. Mixed style of ancient manuscript drawing, cave-art figures and modern line art, soft torn parchment edges, no hard rectangle.
Paul writes with his own hand

A sketch on aged papyrus: an older man with a short gray beard, a chain on one wrist, writing a few large Greek letters at the end of a small sheet, with a coin purse and a wax tablet beside him and a guard's spear at the edge. Loose ink lines, ochre wash, faded edges blending into the scroll.

A playful cave-drawing style panel on parchment: two outlines of the same young man, one hunched and walking away down a road, the other walking back upright with a letter in hand, joined by a curving path and the Greek words ACHRESTOS and EUCHRESTOS lettered along it. Earth tones, soft irregular border.
reading: J. B. Lightfoot, Saint Paul's Epistles to the Colossians and to Philemon (1875)
The classic commentary: the Greek text, notes on every phrase, Apphia and the Phrygian names, Pliny's letter, and an essay on the gospel and slavery. Free online.
Allen Dwight Callahan, Embassy of Onesimus: The Letter of Paul to Philemon (1997)
A short, provocative book arguing that Onesimus was Philemon's estranged brother rather than his slave.
John Knox, Philemon among the Letters of Paul (1935; rev. 1959)
The theory that Onesimus became bishop of Ephesus and helped collect Paul's letters.
Jennifer A. Glancy, Slavery in Early Christianity (2002)
What slavery meant for bodies, households and churches in the world of the New Testament.
J. Albert Harrill, Slaves in the New Testament: Literary, Social, and Moral Dimensions (2006)
A study of the slaves and the language of slavery in the New Testament writings.
